lessons.title: Nutrients and nutrient requirements
lessons.html:
The six nutrient groups

Every ration must supply water, energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and, for ruminants, enough effective fibre. Feed costs are often the largest single expense in a livestock enterprise, so planning nutrition well is one of the biggest levers a manager has on profit.

NutrientRoleTypical SA sources
WaterAll body functions; intake drives feed intakeBoreholes, dams, troughs
EnergyMaintenance, growth, milk, workMaize, veld grass, silage, molasses
ProteinMuscle, milk, wool, rumen microbesOilcake (soya, sunflower, cottonseed), lucerne, urea for ruminants
MineralsBones, enzymes, fertilitySalt, limestone, phosphate licks, trace-mineral premixes
VitaminsMetabolism, immunity, visionGreen forage, premixes
FibreRumen health, ruminationHay, veld, crop residues

Requirements depend on the animal

An animal needs nutrients first for maintenance, then for production: growth, pregnancy, milk, wool or work. A dry, open Nguni cow on veld needs far less than a high-producing Holstein in early lactation. Requirements are published in feeding standards and nutrition tables; a qualified animal nutritionist can formulate rations to them.

Dry matter thinking

Feeds contain different amounts of water. Always compare and formulate on a dry matter (DM) basis. Maize silage may be roughly a third dry matter, while hay is mostly dry matter. A cow eating 30 kg of fresh silage therefore eats far less dry matter than one eating 30 kg of hay. Laboratory analysis of your own feeds gives the most reliable values.

lessons.title: Grazing, licks and supplementation
lessons.html:
Using the veld well

Most South African cattle, sheep and goats depend on natural veld or planted pastures. Sweetveld (common in drier, lower-rainfall areas) stays palatable into winter, while sourveld (higher-rainfall areas such as parts of Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal) loses nutritive value sharply after the growing season. This difference largely determines the supplementation strategy.

Matching supplements to the season

  • Summer (growing season): green grass is usually high in protein and energy but often low in phosphorus. A phosphate lick is commonly used, especially in phosphorus-deficient areas.
  • Winter (dormant season): dry grass is low in protein. A protein or urea-based winter lick helps rumen microbes digest the dry grass, so animals eat more and lose less condition.
  • Production licks: include more energy and protein for pregnant heifers, lactating cows or weaners.

Urea safety

Urea is a cheap nitrogen source for ruminants but is poisonous if animals eat too much quickly. Introduce urea licks gradually, mix thoroughly, keep licks dry, ensure water is always available and never give urea to pigs, poultry or horses. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and your nutritionist's advice exactly.

Body condition scoring

Score animals regularly (for cattle commonly on a 1 to 5 scale). Plan so that cows reach the right condition at calving and mating. Condition lost in winter is expensive to put back, and thin cows conceive late.

Stocking rate

No lick can replace grass that is not there. Match animal numbers to the carrying capacity of the veld, keep a fodder bank of hay or standing foggage for droughts, and plan destocking early when rain fails.

lessons.title: Planning and costing rations
lessons.html:
From requirements to a feed plan

Steps in ration planning

  1. Define the animal group: species, weight, stage, target production.
  2. Look up or obtain requirements for dry matter intake, energy, protein, minerals and fibre.
  3. List available feeds with their analysis and cost per tonne.
  4. Combine feeds so the ration meets requirements at the lowest practical cost (least-cost formulation, often done with software or a nutritionist).
  5. Check practical limits: palatability, maximum inclusion of urea or high-starch grain, effective fibre.
  6. Change rations gradually, typically over one to two weeks, to let rumen microbes adapt.

Costing example

A feedlot compares feeds on cost per unit of nutrient, not cost per tonne. If one protein source costs more per tonne but supplies much more protein, it may be cheaper per kilogram of protein delivered. Track feed conversion ratio (kg feed per kg gain): a lower figure means more efficient use of a costly input.

Feed planning over the year

Build a feed flow budget for the year: estimate monthly demand (animal numbers times intake) against supply from veld, pastures, silage and bought feed. Gaps show where you must plant, store or buy. Budget in ZAR and update when prices or rainfall change.

Feed safety

Store feed dry and rodent-free to avoid mould, which can produce mycotoxins. Check for poisonous plants such as slangkop or tulp in camps, and keep animals away from fertiliser bags and treated seed.

Key points

  • Rations must supply water, energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre on a dry matter basis.
  • Match supplements to the season and veld type.
  • Introduce urea carefully and never feed it to monogastrics.
  • Compare feeds on cost per unit of nutrient.
  • Change diets gradually and plan feed flow for the whole year.
